## Keeping Kefir Consistent Isn’t an Easy Task


For consumers, consistency is largely invisible. A favorite kefir should deliver the same[refreshing taste, texture](https://www.iff.com/media/stories/cultures-shape-kefir/) and level of carbonation every time it is opened. No matter if it was produced yesterday or several weeks earlier. For manufacturers, achieving that predictability is considerably more complicated. Kefir remains biologically active long after the main fermentation stage has finished.


- The microorganisms responsible for the character consumers value can continue to influence acidity, flavor, texture and gas formation during storage.
- Yeast activity that creates an appealing hint of effervescence can become excessive carbonation, while continuing acidification can gradually shift a mild, balanced flavor towards something sharper.
- [Texture](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/dairy-cultures/texture-at-the-core/) must remain appealing throughout shelf life. At the same time, all of this must be achieved while maintaining efficient production at commercial scale.


The challenge, therefore, is not simply making a good kefir. It is making the same good kefir repeatedly. And ensuring that the product consumers experience towards the end of its shelf life remains recognizably close to the one that left the production line.


## Keeping fermentation on track


Consistency starts with acidification. Manufacturers need[cultures](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/) that reach the required pH reliably and within a commercially viable timeframe.


The choice of[culture](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/) can have a significant bearing on that performance, with **IFF’s kefir portfolio** encompassing systems with different acidification speeds, fermentation temperatures and sensory characteristics, depending on the intended product and process. Efficiency matters because fermentation time affects production capacity and cost. However, speed cannot be considered independently of the finished product. A faster process still needs to deliver the required flavor and texture while providing sufficient pH stability during subsequent storage.


This has encouraged the development of[culture](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/) combinations that allow manufacturers to manage several objectives simultaneously, rather than treating acidification, flavor and stability as separate challenges.


> **IFF’s CHOOZIT® KefirMild Plus** , for example, is a multispecies culture developed to combine fast milk fermentation while maintaining high acidification stability at pH 4.5. Its culture composition also includes patented Streptococcus thermophilus strains intended to enhance texture while minimizing post-acidification during fermentation and refrigerated storage.


## When yeast becomes too much of a good thing


Yeast presents perhaps the clearest example of the balancing act involved in kefir production. Its contribution to aroma and carbonation can be essential to the desired kefir character. However, allowing yeast activity to continue unchecked creates a very different proposition.


Excessive yeast development during storage can increase CO₂ production, changing both flavor and the level of fizziness while potentially causing packaging to swell. The challenge becomes particularly important when products are filled into bottles or cups that need to retain their integrity throughout distribution and storage.


Controlling yeast does not necessarily mean eliminating it. Instead, manufacturers can standardize the type and level of yeast according to the desired product and then manage its behavior during cold storage.


> IFF’s DH LYO culture, for example, contains the lactose-negative yeast *Debaryomyces hansenii* , which grows very slowly at 12°C and does not grow in milk at 4°C


The appropriate dosage depends on numerous production variables, including fermentation temperature, milk aeration, cooling speed, maturation, packaging temperature and even package size and filling volume, illustrating how closely culture and process need to work together.


## Building texture in kefir that lasts


Flavor and carbonation may be among kefir’s most distinctive characteristics. But texture is just as important to the consumer experience. Manufacturers need to achieve the desired viscosity and mouthfeel during production. They also need to ensure that those qualities remain stable throughout shelf life.


The solution depends on more than[culture](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/) choice alone. Milk composition, heat treatment, fermentation temperature and processing conditions all influence the finished texture. However, selected texturizing[cultures](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/) can provide manufacturers with an additional tool for managing this complexity.


> **IFF’s TA 480 and TA 490 thermophilic cultures** contain patented strains designed to create higher texture in milk with minimal post-acidification during fermentation and refrigerated storage.


The process remains important, with fermentation temperatures of 28°C or above required to achieve the intended increase in texture. Other adjunct cultures within the portfolio can be used to influence texture alongside fermentation time and flavor, allowing the overall culture system to be configured around the required product characteristics.


## Protecting quality throughout shelf life


The final challenge is ensuring that a product remains stable once it has left the dairy. Cold storage slows microbial activity, but it does not necessarily remove the possibility of yeast development, post-acidification or sensory change.


> Research conducted in IFF’s laboratory in Denmark, supported by market experience, found that **HOLDBAC® YM-B** used at 5-10 DCU per 100 liters of milk can delay yeast development during refrigerated storage.


By inhibiting unwanted yeast growth, it can help manufacturers maintaining product quality and sensory characteristics from the beginning to the end of shelf-life.


The wider IFF adjunct portfolio reflects the fact that there is rarely a single intervention that delivers every required outcome. Different cultures can be selected to support texture, accelerate fermentation, influence flavor, standardize yeast or inhibit unwanted yeast development. This enables manufacturers to build a fermentation system around the particular challenges of their product and production environment.


## Finding the right balance of Kefir


Consistency in kefir is ultimately about balance:


- Retaining enough microbial activity to deliver the flavor and character consumers associate with the category
- Controlling that activity sufficiently to achieve predictable production, stable texture, manageable carbonation and reliable shelf life.
- Looking beyond the starter culture in isolation. Fermentation temperature, cooling, milk composition, packaging and storage conditions all interact with the microorganisms inside the product
-


Therefore, changing one element can have consequences elsewhere in the process.


With more than 80 years of kefir culture expertise, IFF approaches this challenge by helping manufacturers engineer the wider[fermentation](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/dairy-cultures/fresh-fermented/) system around the outcome they need. IFF supports you by drawing on acidifying and texturizing cultures, yeast standardization, cultures with a bioprotective effect and process knowledge rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all solution. Once that foundation of consistency is in place, manufacturers have considerably more freedom to explore what kefir can become.


New flavors, higher protein levels, alternative formats and entirely different consumption occasions all create opportunities for differentiation, but each also introduces new demands on formulation and fermentation. That is where the next stage of the kefir story begins.
